summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for character stream devices such as terminal ports. It was replaced by RFC 1658.

eli5.summary: A checklist of facts you can ask about the ports that send letters and numbers one at a time, like terminal lines.

questions: how do i monitor terminal servers with snmp
subtitle: Standard objects for monitoring character ports and sessions

tldr.problem: Network managers need a standard way to monitor and manage character stream devices like terminal ports, which are common attachment points for non-network devices and virtual consoles.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1316 defines a set of SNMP managed objects organized into port and session tables, allowing managers to inspect and control these devices with standard tools.
tldr.outcome: The Character MIB became part of the standard SNMP framework for equipment that includes terminal interfaces, though it was later replaced by RFC 1658.

today: RFC 1316 is obsoleted by RFC 1658, which provides updated definitions for character stream devices. It should not be used in new implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1316 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing character stream devices. A character stream device is any port that carries character data one at a time, whether physical (like a hardware RS-232 terminal port) or virtual (like a software console port). These include terminal servers, time-sharing hosts with console ports, and parallel printer interfaces.

The RFC treats each port as a first-class managed object with its own status, configuration, and activity counters. It organizes objects into two main tables: one for ports themselves and another for sessions—the virtual connections that carry characters between a port and a partner across the network.
sections.eli5: This is about the telephone lines for old-style terminals. The RFC says what facts you can check: who is logged in, how many characters got sent, whether the flow is stuck.

sections.title: The MIB Architecture
sections.content:
The Character MIB is one of a set of complementary MIBs that work together. The document describes a layered model: at the bottom, physical-level MIBs like the RS-232-like MIB represent the hardware layer (terminal ports, parallel printer ports, and their electrical characteristics). Above that sits the Character MIB, which represents the logical character stream interface. Further above are application-specific MIBs such as the Telnet MIB or PPP MIB, each representing a different use of a character port.

This layering allows the same physical port to be monitored at multiple levels. For example, an RS-232 port can be monitored for electrical characteristics by the RS-232 MIB, for character flow by the Character MIB, and for Telnet protocol details by the Telnet MIB.
sections.eli5: Think of it like layers in a building. The bottom layer is the wires (RS-232). The middle layer is the character stream (this MIB). The top layer is what protocol uses it (Telnet). Each layer has its own dials to check.

sections.title: Port Objects
sections.content:
The Character MIB defines ports as the central abstraction. A physical port corresponds to a hardware connector; a virtual port is a software entity with no hardware. Each port has a unique index and a collection of read-write and read-only properties.

Key port objects include: charPortType (physical or virtual), charPortAdminStatus (enabled, disabled, off, or maintenance), and charPortOperStatus (the actual current state: up, down, maintenance, absent, or active with a user logged in). The RFC also tracks flow control on input and output—whether it is none, XON/XOFF software control, hardware control, or specific RS-232 signals like CTS/RTS.

Port activity is monitored through counters: charPortInCharacters and charPortOutCharacters count the total characters seen on the port since system restart. A port can host multiple sessions, up to a configured maximum.
sections.eli5: A port is a slot where something plugs in. The MIB tells you if it is turned on, if data is moving, and how many characters have gone in and out.

sections.title: Session Objects
sections.content:
A session represents a virtual connection through a port to a remote partner, typically running a protocol like Telnet over TCP. The Character MIB defines a session table with one row per active session, indexed by port and session number.

Session objects track the protocol being used (charSessProtocol—for example, Telnet, Rlogin, LAT, X.29, or VTP), the direction of session establishment (charSessOperOrigin—from network, local, or unknown), and the connection state (charSessState: connecting, connected, or disconnecting). Each session has its own character counters (charSessInCharacters and charSessOutCharacters), which are subsets of the port totals.

A manager can terminate a session by setting the charSessKill object to execute, and can link a session to related MIB information via charSessConnectionId (for example, a pointer to TCP connection state for Telnet).
sections.eli5: A session is a conversation happening on a port. The MIB says which protocol (like Telnet), whether someone started it locally or from the network, and how many characters went back and forth.

sections.title: Status
sections.content:
RFC 1316 was published in April 1992 as a Proposed Standard. The document notes that security issues are not discussed in the memo. This is an older document predating modern security practices in SNMP.

RFC 1316 has been obsoleted by RFC 1658, which provides updated definitions for character stream devices. The Character MIB as defined here should not be used in new implementations; RFC 1658 is the current standard.
sections.eli5: This RFC is old (1992) and no longer used. RFC 1658 took its place and added more things to check.
